definition.text: The environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things.

facts.text: It contrasts with anthropocentrism, centred on humans, and sentientism, which values only beings that can feel pleasure or pain; ecocentrism extends value to the whole of nature.
Its four pillars: humans and other species share Earth's community, all species are interdependent, each organism pursues its own good, and humans are not inherently superior.
It includes Albert Schweitzer's 'reverence for life', Peter Singer's animal liberation and Paul W. Taylor's biocentric egalitarianism.
Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, animal rights and environmental protection.
Critics call it anti-human and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.
The US Endangered Species Act has been described as unusually biocentric for putting non-human species first.

definition.text: The legal recognition of nature as having rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law.

facts.text: Ecuador was the first country to put rights of nature in its constitution, in 2008.
Its Article 71 gives nature the right to respect for its existence and the regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions and evolution.
Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia adopted rights-of-nature laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.

title: Deep ecology

definition.text: An environmental philosophy holding that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match.

facts.text: Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish, independent of human use.
Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss first used the phrase in a 1973 article.
Næss contrasted it with 'shallow ecology', which he criticised as utilitarian, human-centred and consumer-oriented.
It rejects the view of nature as a resource to exploit and holds that the materialist paradigm, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced.
Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring is often seen as the start of the movement.
Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores overconsumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic.
Arguments about the non-market valuation of ecosystems draw on environmental ethics and deep ecology.

contested_note: Critics call it Eurocentric, misanthropic or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge.

definition.text: A nature-centred rather than human-centred system of values.

facts.text: It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only or greater bearers of intrinsic value.
Aldo Leopold conceived the ethic, and his land ethic is central to it.
It values the biotic community as a whole and aims to keep ecosystem composition and processes intact, covering living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone.
Supporters argue that human-centred ethics makes protecting nature always depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives it a firmer basis.
Critics argue it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

definition.text: A set of values centred on technology, holding that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science.

facts.text: Technocentrics accept that environmental problems exist but do not see cutting industry as the solution.
Ecocentrics, by contrast, see themselves as subject to nature and prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.
